Every MLB The Show game since MLB 06 has put at least one star on the box. This page lists every cover athlete from MLB 06: The Show through MLB The Show 26, newest first, plus the special edition and regional covers, and what we know so far about MLB The Show 27.
Looking for the in-game cards instead? Every Cover Athlete Series card we track is on our Cover Athletes card series page.

## How MLB The Show Picks Its Cover Athlete
San Diego Studio (SDS) picks one main cover athlete each year, and it's usually a player coming off a big season. Dustin Pedroia (MLB 09), Joe Mauer (MLB 10), Josh Donaldson (MLB The Show 16) and Shohei Ohtani (MLB The Show 22) were all reigning American League MVPs when they got the cover.
It isn't only about stats. When SDS announced Vladimir Guerrero Jr. for MLB The Show 24, it said it looks for "great baseball players who have interesting stories to tell" and people "who genuinely enjoy playing MLB The Show."
The reveal also marks the start of the new game's pre-release cycle. The cover announcement usually comes with the release date, and the special edition reveal follows a few days later.

## Every MLB The Show Cover Athlete, Year by Year
This table lists the main (standard edition, U.S.) cover for every game. Special edition and regional covers are in the tables below it.

The MLB The Show covers run from David Ortiz on MLB 06 The Show to Aaron Judge on MLB The Show 26. Judge is the first player since Joe Mauer to return as the primary United States cover athlete, while MLB The Show 25 became the first main cover built around three active players.
The complete chronology comes first. The ranking then preserves the original 17 cover seasons from worst to best, using production during the cover year, the season that earned the selection, postseason value, and some unavoidable personal judgment. Retired legends used only for special editions are listed in the history but are not judged as contemporary cover seasons.

## MLB The Show covers by year

This list focuses on the primary North American artwork. Several releases had separate Canadian, Taiwanese, or Korean athletes, including Russell Martin, Jose Bautista, Wei Yin Chen, and Shin Soo Choo. The series also existed before The Show name, with Vladimir Guerrero Sr on MLB 2006 immediately before the modern naming era began.

## How the cover athletes are ranked
I give the most weight to the player’s performance during the season attached to the cover. The prior season matters because it usually explains the selection, and the following season can add context without overriding what happened during the cover year.
Ken Griffey Jr, Jackie Robinson, and Derek Jeter are excluded from the competitive ranking because their special covers celebrated completed careers. The three athletes on the 2025 cover and Judge’s 2026 return are kept in the chronology, while the ranking below preserves the completed 17 entry comparison that began with MLB 06 and ran through MLB The Show 23.

## MLB The Show cover athlete ranking
### 17) Javier Baez in MLB The Show 20
Baez lands last because the shortened 2020 season went badly both statistically and emotionally. He hit .203 with a .599 OPS across 59 games, a sharp fall from the energetic all around play that made him such a marketable selection. The unusual schedule makes every 2020 comparison imperfect, but the cover season never developed into a convincing success.

## MLB The Show cover athlete ranking
### 16) Jazz Chisholm Jr in MLB The Show 23
San Diego Studio took a reasonable swing on an exciting young player coming off a 2022 All Star selection. Injuries again interrupted Chisholm’s progress, however, and he played only 97 games in 2023. He still approached a 20 home run and 20 stolen base season, so I would call this a miss in timing rather than proof that the player lacked cover appeal.

## MLB The Show cover athlete ranking
### 15) Yasiel Puig in MLB 15 The Show
Puig had already produced an All Star caliber 2014 season worth roughly five wins above replacement, which made the choice less reckless than it can look in hindsight. He appeared in only 79 games in 2015 and posted a .758 OPS. The energy, Los Angeles market, and breakout potential all made sense, but the actual cover year failed to deliver.

## MLB The Show cover athlete ranking
### 14) Joe Mauer in MLB 11 The Show
Mauer received a second consecutive cover, but the second season was the difficult one. Injuries limited him to 82 games, and his production declined across the board. His peak had already justified the larger relationship with the series, yet MLB 11 was the weaker of his two individual cover cases.

## MLB The Show cover athlete ranking
### 13) Adrian Gonzalez in MLB 12 The Show
Gonzalez was pictured in a Boston uniform and ended the season with the Dodgers, which immediately made the artwork feel dated. He still drove in 108 runs and finished with an .806 OPS, but those numbers were modest by his own standard. I also think the selection arrived after his most memorable years in San Diego rather than at the center of his peak.

## MLB The Show cover athlete ranking
### 12) Bryce Harper in MLB The Show 19
Harper’s move from Washington to Philadelphia gave the cover enormous marketing value. His 2019 line included 35 home runs, 114 RBI, an .882 OPS, and about four wins above replacement, but the Phillies finished at .500. It was a strong season for most players and a merely good one for Harper, which keeps the cover in the lower half.

## MLB The Show cover athlete ranking
### 11) Aaron Judge in MLB The Show 18
Judge earned the cover with a historic rookie season that included 52 home runs, Rookie of the Year, and second place in MVP voting. A wrist injury limited him to 112 games in 2018, but he still hit 27 home runs, posted a .919 OPS, and played well in October. The missed time caps the ranking even though the choice itself was excellent.

## MLB The Show cover athlete ranking
### 10) Fernando Tatis Jr in MLB The Show 21
Tatis led the National League with 42 home runs, produced a .975 OPS, and finished third in MVP voting while playing 130 games. San Diego missed the postseason, and later injury and suspension changed the way the period is remembered. Judged only on the 2021 cover year, this was still a well timed selection with elite power at shortstop.

## MLB The Show cover athlete ranking
### 9) Joe Mauer in MLB 10 The Show
Mauer entered the cover year after an extraordinary 2009 MVP season in which he hit .365 with a .444 on base percentage and 1.031 OPS. He remained an elite offensive catcher in 2010, hitting .327 with an .871 OPS and finishing eighth in MVP voting. Combining those two seasons makes the first Mauer cover far stronger than the second.

## MLB The Show cover athlete ranking
### 8) Dustin Pedroia in MLB 09 The Show
Pedroia earned the selection with a 2008 MVP season that included 213 hits, 54 doubles, 118 runs, 20 stolen bases, and roughly seven wins above replacement. His 2009 follow up was less spectacular but still valuable, with an .819 OPS and another strong all around season at second base. The cover caught him near the heart of his peak.

## MLB The Show cover athlete ranking
### 7) Ryan Howard in MLB 08 The Show
Howard led the majors with 48 home runs and 146 RBI, finished second in National League MVP voting, and helped Philadelphia win the 2008 World Series. His on base percentage and defense prevent the season from rating as highly by modern all around measures, but a championship cover year with that much power deserves a prominent place.

## MLB The Show cover athlete ranking
### 6) Miguel Cabrera in MLB 14 The Show
Cabrera entered 2014 after consecutive MVP awards and the 2012 Triple Crown. The cover season looked quiet only beside that impossible standard: he hit .313 with 25 home runs, 109 RBI, and an .895 OPS while Detroit won its division. I cannot put him lower when the selection represented one of the greatest modern hitting runs.

# 'MLB The Show 26' announces it will 'not have a new cover athlete' for this year's version of the game
Chris CwikContributing writer
Mon, Jan 26, 2026·
4 min read
5
The "MLB The Show" cover reveal is always a highly anticipated offseason announcement. Fans of the video game are always eager to see which up-and-coming, exciting star or legendary player will grace its cover.
With the 2026 MLB season closer than you might think, "MLB The Show 26" announced Monday that the game will not feature a "new cover athlete" this year.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
That announcement was made in a short statement, which read:
> "To our MLB The Show community:
> "First off, we at San Diego Studios want to thank you, the MLB The Show Community, for your continued support and feedback.
> "We know that you are all just as excited as we are for the release of MLB The Show 26, so we wanted to let everyone know that this year we have decided that we will not have a new cover athlete.
> "Please stay tuned to all of our social channels for more information to come."
That statement drew plenty of questions. With no "new cover athlete" this year, what or who will grace the cover this time around? The MLB logo? A generic baseball? Rob Manfred? As San Diego Studios teased, fans will have to keep an eye on "MLB The Show" social media channels for more information.
That last statement, combined with the word "new" appearing in the release, should inject a healthy amount of skepticism in Monday's announcement. With the Super Bowl coming up, brands can't be trusted. Celebrity chef Guy Fieri went viral recently for showing off a "new look" just prior to the Super Bowl. Are you really going to buy that?
Even if this isn't a huge misdirect by "MLB The Show," the presence of the word "new" is carrying a lot of weight. It's possible a returning cover athlete will appear on the cover for a second time. Or it's possible the game will go with some sort of montage featuring multiple former cover athletes. There's enough ambiguity here to suspect the people over at "MLB The Show 26" have something up their sleeves.

Madden also did it in "Madden 22," when Patrick Mahomes and Tom Brady graced the cover together.

## How MLB The Show Picks Its Cover Athlete
San Diego Studio (SDS) picks one main cover athlete each year, and it's usually a player coming off a big season. Dustin Pedroia (MLB 09), Joe Mauer (MLB 10), Josh Donaldson (MLB The Show 16) and Shohei Ohtani (MLB The Show 22) were all reigning American League MVPs when they got the cover.
It isn't only about stats. When SDS announced Vladimir Guerrero Jr. for MLB The Show 24, it said it looks for "great baseball players who have interesting stories to tell" and people "who genuinely enjoy playing MLB The Show."
The reveal also marks the start of the new game's pre-release cycle. The cover announcement usually comes with the release date, and the special edition reveal follows a few days later.

The MLB The Show covers run from David Ortiz on MLB 06 The Show to Aaron Judge on MLB The Show 26. Judge is the first player since Joe Mauer to return as the primary United States cover athlete, while MLB The Show 25 became the first main cover built around three active players.
The complete chronology comes first. The ranking then preserves the original 17 cover seasons from worst to best, using production during the cover year, the season that earned the selection, postseason value, and some unavoidable personal judgment. Retired legends used only for special editions are listed in the history but are not judged as contemporary cover seasons.

## How the cover athletes are ranked
I give the most weight to the player’s performance during the season attached to the cover. The prior season matters because it usually explains the selection, and the following season can add context without overriding what happened during the cover year.
Ken Griffey Jr, Jackie Robinson, and Derek Jeter are excluded from the competitive ranking because their special covers celebrated completed careers. The three athletes on the 2025 cover and Judge’s 2026 return are kept in the chronology, while the ranking below preserves the completed 17 entry comparison that began with MLB 06 and ran through MLB The Show 23.
texts.3:
## MLB The Show cover athlete ranking
### 17) Javier Baez in MLB The Show 20
Baez lands last because the shortened 2020 season went badly both statistically and emotionally. He hit .203 with a .599 OPS across 59 games, a sharp fall from the energetic all around play that made him such a marketable selection. The unusual schedule makes every 2020 comparison imperfect, but the cover season never developed into a convincing success.
texts.4:
## MLB The Show cover athlete ranking
### 16) Jazz Chisholm Jr in MLB The Show 23
San Diego Studio took a reasonable swing on an exciting young player coming off a 2022 All Star selection. Injuries again interrupted Chisholm’s progress, however, and he played only 97 games in 2023. He still approached a 20 home run and 20 stolen base season, so I would call this a miss in timing rather than proof that the player lacked cover appeal.
texts.5:
## MLB The Show cover athlete ranking
### 15) Yasiel Puig in MLB 15 The Show
Puig had already produced an All Star caliber 2014 season worth roughly five wins above replacement, which made the choice less reckless than it can look in hindsight. He appeared in only 79 games in 2015 and posted a .758 OPS. The energy, Los Angeles market, and breakout potential all made sense, but the actual cover year failed to deliver.
texts.6:
## MLB The Show cover athlete ranking
### 14) Joe Mauer in MLB 11 The Show
Mauer received a second consecutive cover, but the second season was the difficult one. Injuries limited him to 82 games, and his production declined across the board. His peak had already justified the larger relationship with the series, yet MLB 11 was the weaker of his two individual cover cases.
texts.7:
## MLB The Show cover athlete ranking
### 13) Adrian Gonzalez in MLB 12 The Show
Gonzalez was pictured in a Boston uniform and ended the season with the Dodgers, which immediately made the artwork feel dated. He still drove in 108 runs and finished with an .806 OPS, but those numbers were modest by his own standard. I also think the selection arrived after his most memorable years in San Diego rather than at the center of his peak.
texts.8:
## MLB The Show cover athlete ranking
### 12) Bryce Harper in MLB The Show 19
Harper’s move from Washington to Philadelphia gave the cover enormous marketing value. His 2019 line included 35 home runs, 114 RBI, an .882 OPS, and about four wins above replacement, but the Phillies finished at .500. It was a strong season for most players and a merely good one for Harper, which keeps the cover in the lower half.
texts.9:
## MLB The Show cover athlete ranking
### 11) Aaron Judge in MLB The Show 18
Judge earned the cover with a historic rookie season that included 52 home runs, Rookie of the Year, and second place in MVP voting. A wrist injury limited him to 112 games in 2018, but he still hit 27 home runs, posted a .919 OPS, and played well in October. The missed time caps the ranking even though the choice itself was excellent.
texts.10:
## MLB The Show cover athlete ranking
### 10) Fernando Tatis Jr in MLB The Show 21
Tatis led the National League with 42 home runs, produced a .975 OPS, and finished third in MVP voting while playing 130 games. San Diego missed the postseason, and later injury and suspension changed the way the period is remembered. Judged only on the 2021 cover year, this was still a well timed selection with elite power at shortstop.
texts.11:
## MLB The Show cover athlete ranking
### 9) Joe Mauer in MLB 10 The Show
Mauer entered the cover year after an extraordinary 2009 MVP season in which he hit .365 with a .444 on base percentage and 1.031 OPS. He remained an elite offensive catcher in 2010, hitting .327 with an .871 OPS and finishing eighth in MVP voting. Combining those two seasons makes the first Mauer cover far stronger than the second.
texts.12:
## MLB The Show cover athlete ranking
### 8) Dustin Pedroia in MLB 09 The Show
Pedroia earned the selection with a 2008 MVP season that included 213 hits, 54 doubles, 118 runs, 20 stolen bases, and roughly seven wins above replacement. His 2009 follow up was less spectacular but still valuable, with an .819 OPS and another strong all around season at second base. The cover caught him near the heart of his peak.
texts.13:
## MLB The Show cover athlete ranking
### 7) Ryan Howard in MLB 08 The Show
Howard led the majors with 48 home runs and 146 RBI, finished second in National League MVP voting, and helped Philadelphia win the 2008 World Series. His on base percentage and defense prevent the season from rating as highly by modern all around measures, but a championship cover year with that much power deserves a prominent place.
texts.14:
## MLB The Show cover athlete ranking
### 6) Miguel Cabrera in MLB 14 The Show
Cabrera entered 2014 after consecutive MVP awards and the 2012 Triple Crown. The cover season looked quiet only beside that impossible standard: he hit .313 with 25 home runs, 109 RBI, and an .895 OPS while Detroit won its division. I cannot put him lower when the selection represented one of the greatest modern hitting runs.

**David Allen Wright** (born December 20, 1982) is an American former professional baseballthird baseman who spent his entire 14-year Major League Baseball (MLB) career with the New York Mets. Chosen by the Mets in the 2001 MLB draft, he made his MLB debut on July 21, 2004 at Shea Stadium. Internationally, Wright represented the United States. Wright was nicknamed "**Captain America**" after his performance in the 2013 World Baseball Classic where he led the tournament with 10 RBI and a .438 batting average and was named to the All-World Baseball Classic Team.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wright#cite_note-1)

Wright is a seven-time All-Star, a two-time Gold Glove Award winner, a two-time Silver Slugger Award winner, and a member of the 30–30 club. One of the most beloved players in franchise history, Wright is the Mets' all-time leader in career plate appearances and holds many other franchise records for position players. He was named captain of the Mets in 2013, becoming the fourth captain in the team's history. Wright is the third player to play in at least 10 MLB seasons and play his entire MLB career with the Mets.
Throughout the latter half of Wright's career, he was plagued by injuries, most notably spinal stenosis, as well as additional ailments in his neck and shoulder. After missing significant time from 2015 to 2018 and receiving word from doctors that his spinal stenosis would not improve, Wright announced that 2018 would be his final season as an active player. Wright finished his major league career with a .296 career batting average, 242 home runs, and 970 runs batted in.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wright#cite_note-2) Upon completion of his playing career, Wright was named a special advisor in the Mets front office.
Wright (right) and Michael Cuddyer played baseball together as children in Virginia before playing together on the Mets in 2015.

David Allen Wright was born on December 20, 1982, in Norfolk, Virginia, the oldest of four sons of Rhon, a police officer in the Norfolk Police Department, and Elisa Wright.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wright#cite_note-dad-3) Wright grew up a Mets fan due to his proximity to the Class AAANorfolk Tides, whose stadium was ten minutes from his home.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wright#cite_note-4) Wright took hitting lessons alongside fellow future Major Leaguer Michael Cuddyer in elementary school and played on teams with Ryan Zimmerman, Mark Reynolds, B. J. Upton and Justin Upton during high school.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wright#cite_note-5) Wright played baseball at Hickory High School in Chesapeake, Virginia. He committed to play college baseball at Georgia Tech before his senior year of high school. As a high school senior, he had a .538 batting average.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wright#cite_note-6)

## Professional career
[edit]

## Professional career
### Draft and minor leagues
[edit]
The New York Mets selected Wright in the 2001 MLB draft during the supplemental round as compensation for the Mets' loss of Mike Hampton to the Colorado Rockies in free agency. Wright was selected after future teammate Aaron Heilman, who had been selected in the first round.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wright#cite_note-7) According to then-Mets manager Bobby Valentine, Wright had caught the attention of coach Tom Robson who had actually been sent "down to Virginia to scout someone else."[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wright#cite_note-8)
Wright progressed steadily in his first three years of minor league play, winning the Sterling award for best player on the class A St. Lucie Mets in 2003. In 2004, he quickly rose from the Double-ABinghamton Mets to the Triple-ANorfolk Tides to the major leagues.

## Professional career
### New York Mets (2004–2016, 2018)
[edit]
On July 21, 2004, Wright made his major league debut starting at third base against the Montreal Expos at Shea Stadium. The next day, Wright picked up his first career hit, a double off of Expos' pitcher Zach Day. On July 26, Wright hit his first major league home run, a solo blast off of pitcher John Patterson. Wright finished his rookie season with a .293 batting average, 14 home runs, and 40 RBI in 263 at-bats in 69 games, and was voted as the This Year in Baseball Awards Rookie of the Year.
Wright made an over-the-shoulder barehanded catch during the seventh inning of a game at Petco Park against the San Diego Padres on August 9, 2005. With one out in the inning, Brian Giles hit a broken-bat blooper 20 feet (6.1 m) beyond the edge of the outfield grass. Wright, retreating quickly with his back to home plate, extended his bare right hand and caught the ball cleanly while crashing to the field. Wright maintained control of the ball after landing hard on the outfield grass. The sellout crowd at Petco Park acknowledged the splendor of the catch with a standing ovation lasting several minutes. This play was voted the "This Year in Baseball Play of the Year."[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wright#cite_note-TYIB-9)

## Professional career
### New York Mets (2004–2016, 2018)
In 2005, the 22-year-old Wright played in 160 games and batted .306 with 27 home runs, 102 RBIs, 99 runs scored, 42 doubles, and 17 stolen bases, leading the team in average, runs, on-base percentage, slugging percentage, RBI, doubles, and finishing second in home runs to Cliff Floyd (34). Wright was also in the top 10 in the National League for average, hits, total bases, RBI, extra-base hits, and runs. However, his 24 errors tied him with Troy Glaus for the most errors by a third baseman in the major leagues.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wright#cite_note-espn-error-10)
Wright with the Mets in 2006
In 2006, Wright was named National League Co-Player of the Week for June 12–18 along with teammate José Reyes.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wright#cite_note-PlayerOfTheWeek-11) For the month, Wright batted .327 with 10 home runs and 29 RBIs.

## Professional career
### New York Mets (2004–2016, 2018)
Wright also provided his share of heroics throughout the 2006 season. His first game-winning hit occurred on May 5 with a 2-out double just out of the reach of a chasing Andruw Jones in the bottom of the 14th inning off Jorge Sosa to defeat the Atlanta Braves, 8–7. Two weeks later on May 19, he hit a walk-off single off Yankees closer Mariano Rivera that just sailed over the head of center fielder Johnny Damon as the Mets rallied to beat the Yankees in the first game of the 2006 Subway Series, 7–6. He capped off the month on Memorial Day, May 29, with a single to the wall in left-center field off Arizona Diamondbacks closer José Valverde scoring José Reyes from first base as the Mets defeated Arizona, 8–7. Wright also made a game-saving stop at third base of a would-be game-tying single by Mike Lieberthal for the final out of a 4–3 Mets victory over the Philadelphia Phillies on August 5.
Wright was voted into his first MLB All-Star Game as the starting third baseman for the NL. During the 2006 season, Wright collected 74 RBIs before the All-Star break, breaking the Mets record previously held by Mike Piazza, who had 72 RBIs in 2000. Wright also participated in the 2006 Home Run Derby, reaching the final round but finishing second to Ryan Howard of the Philadelphia Phillies. He hit 22 home runs in the contest, including 16 in the first round, the third-highest total in any one round in the history of the Home Run Derby.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wright#cite_note-SIHRDerby-12) The following night, he hit a home run in his first All-Star Game at-bat off American League starter Kenny Rogers.

## Professional career
### New York Mets (2004–2016, 2018)
Wright ranked among the club's top three hitters in all offensive categories for the 2006 Mets, who were the second most run-scoring team in the National League. Fans at Shea Stadium have routinely greeted Wright's performances with chants of "M-V-P, M-V-P." According to then-teammate Tom Glavine, "He's probably been our most clutch hitter over the first half of the season and he's certainly thrown his hat into the MVP talks."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wright#cite_note-MVPtalk-13)
On August 6, 2006, Wright signed a 6-year, $55 million contract extension with the Mets, as well as a $1.5 million signing bonus. The contract paid him $1 million in 2007, $5 million in 2008, $7.5 million in 2009, $10 million in 2010, $14 million in 2011, and $15 million in 2012. The contract also contained a club option for 2013 worth $16 million. Wright has already announced that he will donate $1.5 million to the Mets Foundation throughout this contract.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wright#cite_note-contract-14)
The Mets clinched the NL East title in 2006 and returned to the playoffs for the first time since 2000. Wright finished the 2006 season batting .311 with 26 home runs, 116 RBI, 40 doubles, and 20 stolen bases in 154 games played. However, he struggled in his first postseason, going 4-for-25 (.160) in the Mets' NLCS loss to the St. Louis Cardinals, and batting .216 in 10 postseason games.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wright#cite_note-15)
After the season, Wright participated in the 2006 MLB Japan All-Star Series along with teammates José Reyes, Julio Franco, and John Maine.

## Professional career
### New York Mets (2004–2016, 2018)
As of April 21, 2007, Wright had a hitting streak of 26 regular-season games; the previous team record was 24, held by Mike Piazza and Hubie Brooks. He had a hit in the 12 final regular-season games of the 2006 season, and had a hit in all of the first 14 games of the 2007 season.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wright#cite_note-16) Wright's hit streak of 26 regular-season games ended on April 21, 2007, against the Atlanta Braves at Shea Stadium.
On September 16, 2007, Wright became the 29th player in baseball history to join the 30–30 club, after hitting a 7th inning solo home run against the Philadelphia Phillies at Shea Stadium. He is only the third player to reach this milestone before his 25th birthday, and only the third Met to reach this milestone in club history, the other two being Howard Johnson and Darryl Strawberry.
Wright finished the 2007 season with a .325 batting average, 30 home runs, 107 RBI, and 34 stolen bases. He was awarded the 2007 Gold Glove and the Silver Slugger Award at third base. Wright also was fourth in the NL MVP voting receiving 182 votes.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wright#cite_note-17)
Wright with the Mets in 2008
Wright began the year with two doubles, including a bases-clearing double, in finishing 2–4 with three RBIs in the Mets' Opening Day victory over the Florida Marlins, 7–2. With the RBIs, Wright was already halfway to matching his RBI production from the preceding April. In the final game of the series, Wright went 3–5 with a home run. On April 13, 2008, Wright hit his 100th career home run, a solo shot off of Milwaukee Brewers pitcher Jeff Suppan.

## Professional career
### New York Mets (2004–2016, 2018)
On August 7, Wright hit the first walk-off home run of his career against the San Diego Padres, giving the Mets a 5–3 victory.
On November 5, Wright was announced as the recipient of the Gold Glove Award for third basemen. It was the second consecutive year in which Wright won the award. His teammate, Carlos Beltrán, also won the award for center fielders. He also won his second Silver Slugger Award.
On December 22, Wright was announced as a member of Team USA in the 2009 World Baseball Classic (WBC) to be held in March 2009. The third base position was taken by Alex Rodriguez in the 2006 WBC.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wright#cite_note-18)
Wright finished seventh in the voting for the 2008 NL MVP award after finishing the season with a .302 batting average, 33 home runs and 124 RBI.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wright#cite_note-19)
On April 13, 2009, Wright hit the first Mets home run in Citi Field history on Opening Day. The three-run homer was hit off San Diego Padres pitcher Walter Silva in the 5th inning.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wright#cite_note-20)
In mid-August, when 10 Mets players were on the disabled list, Wright was added to the list after sustaining an injury on August 15. Wright suffered a concussion when he was hit in the head with a 93 mph (150 km/h)fastball by San Francisco Giants pitcher Matt Cain. He was admitted to the Hospital for Special Surgery, where he underwent a precautionary CT scan, which turned out negative.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wright#cite_note-21) The following day, he left the hospital diagnosed with post-concussion symptoms. He was then placed on the disabled list for the first time in his career.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wright#cite_note-22)

## Professional career
### New York Mets (2004–2016, 2018)
Despite the injury to Wright, General Manager Omar Minaya stated that there were no plans to shut him down for the remainder of the season.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wright#cite_note-23) In fact, Wright was activated from the disabled list on September 1 and started at third base against the Colorado Rockies that evening. In that game, Wright wore a new style of batting helmet (the Rawlings S100). He abandoned that helmet after wearing it in that one game. Wright explained that he found the helmet uncomfortable. "It's the last thing I need to be worrying about in the box is trying to shove it on my head. So I wanted to go back to the old one and just wait to see if there's going to be any adjustments made."[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wright#cite_note-24) Wright experienced a decline in production after a potent campaign in 2008. His home run total dropped to 10, while his RBI total fell to 72, after hitting 33 home runs and 124 RBIs the previous season.
Wright, along with José Reyes, arrived at the Mets' spring training camp in Port St. Lucie, Florida two weeks early to get a head start on preparing themselves after a disappointing 2009 campaign. Wright came into camp heavier than he was in previous seasons, adding more muscle to his body.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wright#cite_note-25)
Wright with the Mets in 2011

## Professional career
### New York Mets (2004–2016, 2018)
On Opening Day, Wright hit a two-run home run off Marlins' pitcher Josh Johnson in his first at-bat of the season. **David Allen Wright** (born December 20, 1982) is an American former professional baseballthird baseman who spent his entire 14-year Major League Baseball (MLB) career with the New York Mets. Chosen by the Mets in the 2001 MLB draft, he made his MLB debut on July 21, 2004 at Shea Stadium. Internationally, Wright represented the United States. Wright was nicknamed "**Captain America**" after his performance in the 2013 World Baseball Classic where he led the tournament with 10 RBI and a .438 batting average and was named to the All-World Baseball Classic Team.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wright#cite_note-1)
texts.1:
Wright is a seven-time All-Star, a two-time Gold Glove Award winner, a two-time Silver Slugger Award winner, and a member of the 30–30 club. One of the most beloved players in franchise history, Wright is the Mets' all-time leader in career plate appearances and holds many other franchise records for position players. He was named captain of the Mets in 2013, becoming the fourth captain in the team's history. Wright is the third player to play in at least 10 MLB seasons and play his entire MLB career with the Mets.
Throughout the latter half of Wright's career, he was plagued by injuries, most notably spinal stenosis, as well as additional ailments in his neck and shoulder. After missing significant time from 2015 to 2018 and receiving word from doctors that his spinal stenosis would not improve, Wright announced that 2018 would be his final season as an active player. Wright finished his major league career with a .296 career batting average, 242 home runs, and 970 runs batted in.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wright#cite_note-2) Upon completion of his playing career, Wright was named a special advisor in the Mets front office.
Wright (right) and Michael Cuddyer played baseball together as children in Virginia before playing together on the Mets in 2015.
texts.2: David Allen Wright was born on December 20, 1982, in Norfolk, Virginia, the oldest of four sons of Rhon, a police officer in the Norfolk Police Department, and Elisa Wright.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wright#cite_note-dad-3) Wright grew up a Mets fan due to his proximity to the Class AAANorfolk Tides, whose stadium was ten minutes from his home.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wright#cite_note-4) Wright took hitting lessons alongside fellow future Major Leaguer Michael Cuddyer in elementary school and played on teams with Ryan Zimmerman, Mark Reynolds, B. J. Upton and Justin Upton during high school.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wright#cite_note-5) Wright played baseball at Hickory High School in Chesapeake, Virginia. He committed to play college baseball at Georgia Tech before his senior year of high school. As a high school senior, he had a .538 batting average.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wright#cite_note-6)

## Professional career
### Draft and minor leagues
[edit]
The New York Mets selected Wright in the 2001 MLB draft during the supplemental round as compensation for the Mets' loss of Mike Hampton to the Colorado Rockies in free agency. Wright was selected after future teammate Aaron Heilman, who had been selected in the first round.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wright#cite_note-7) According to then-Mets manager Bobby Valentine, Wright had caught the attention of coach Tom Robson who had actually been sent "down to Virginia to scout someone else."[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wright#cite_note-8)
Wright progressed steadily in his first three years of minor league play, winning the Sterling award for best player on the class A St. Lucie Mets in 2003. In 2004, he quickly rose from the Double-ABinghamton Mets to the Triple-ANorfolk Tides to the major leagues.

## Professional career
### New York Mets (2004–2016, 2018)
[edit]
On July 21, 2004, Wright made his major league debut starting at third base against the Montreal Expos at Shea Stadium. The next day, Wright picked up his first career hit, a double off of Expos' pitcher Zach Day. On July 26, Wright hit his first major league home run, a solo blast off of pitcher John Patterson. Wright finished his rookie season with a .293 batting average, 14 home runs, and 40 RBI in 263 at-bats in 69 games, and was voted as the This Year in Baseball Awards Rookie of the Year.
Wright made an over-the-shoulder barehanded catch during the seventh inning of a game at Petco Park against the San Diego Padres on August 9, 2005. With one out in the inning, Brian Giles hit a broken-bat blooper 20 feet (6.1 m) beyond the edge of the outfield grass. Wright, retreating quickly with his back to home plate, extended his bare right hand and caught the ball cleanly while crashing to the field. Wright maintained control of the ball after landing hard on the outfield grass. The sellout crowd at Petco Park acknowledged the splendor of the catch with a standing ovation lasting several minutes. This play was voted the "This Year in Baseball Play of the Year."[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wright#cite_note-TYIB-9)

## Professional career
### New York Mets (2004–2016, 2018)
In 2005, the 22-year-old Wright played in 160 games and batted .306 with 27 home runs, 102 RBIs, 99 runs scored, 42 doubles, and 17 stolen bases, leading the team in average, runs, on-base percentage, slugging percentage, RBI, doubles, and finishing second in home runs to Cliff Floyd (34). Wright was also in the top 10 in the National League for average, hits, total bases, RBI, extra-base hits, and runs. However, his 24 errors tied him with Troy Glaus for the most errors by a third baseman in the major leagues.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wright#cite_note-espn-error-10)
Wright with the Mets in 2006
In 2006, Wright was named National League Co-Player of the Week for June 12–18 along with teammate José Reyes.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wright#cite_note-PlayerOfTheWeek-11) For the month, Wright batted .327 with 10 home runs and 29 RBIs.

## Professional career
### New York Mets (2004–2016, 2018)
Wright also provided his share of heroics throughout the 2006 season. His first game-winning hit occurred on May 5 with a 2-out double just out of the reach of a chasing Andruw Jones in the bottom of the 14th inning off Jorge Sosa to defeat the Atlanta Braves, 8–7. Two weeks later on May 19, he hit a walk-off single off Yankees closer Mariano Rivera that just sailed over the head of center fielder Johnny Damon as the Mets rallied to beat the Yankees in the first game of the 2006 Subway Series, 7–6. He capped off the month on Memorial Day, May 29, with a single to the wall in left-center field off Arizona Diamondbacks closer José Valverde scoring José Reyes from first base as the Mets defeated Arizona, 8–7. Wright also made a game-saving stop at third base of a would-be game-tying single by Mike Lieberthal for the final out of a 4–3 Mets victory over the Philadelphia Phillies on August 5.
Wright was voted into his first MLB All-Star Game as the starting third baseman for the NL. During the 2006 season, Wright collected 74 RBIs before the All-Star break, breaking the Mets record previously held by Mike Piazza, who had 72 RBIs in 2000. Wright also participated in the 2006 Home Run Derby, reaching the final round but finishing second to Ryan Howard of the Philadelphia Phillies. He hit 22 home runs in the contest, including 16 in the first round, the third-highest total in any one round in the history of the Home Run Derby.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wright#cite_note-SIHRDerby-12) The following night, he hit a home run in his first All-Star Game at-bat off American League starter Kenny Rogers.
texts.8:
## Professional career
### New York Mets (2004–2016, 2018)
Wright ranked among the club's top three hitters in all offensive categories for the 2006 Mets, who were the second most run-scoring team in the National League. Fans at Shea Stadium have routinely greeted Wright's performances with chants of "M-V-P, M-V-P." According to then-teammate Tom Glavine, "He's probably been our most clutch hitter over the first half of the season and he's certainly thrown his hat into the MVP talks."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wright#cite_note-MVPtalk-13)
On August 6, 2006, Wright signed a 6-year, $55 million contract extension with the Mets, as well as a $1.5 million signing bonus. The contract paid him $1 million in 2007, $5 million in 2008, $7.5 million in 2009, $10 million in 2010, $14 million in 2011, and $15 million in 2012. The contract also contained a club option for 2013 worth $16 million. Wright has already announced that he will donate $1.5 million to the Mets Foundation throughout this contract.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wright#cite_note-contract-14)
The Mets clinched the NL East title in 2006 and returned to the playoffs for the first time since 2000. Wright finished the 2006 season batting .311 with 26 home runs, 116 RBI, 40 doubles, and 20 stolen bases in 154 games played. However, he struggled in his first postseason, going 4-for-25 (.160) in the Mets' NLCS loss to the St. Louis Cardinals, and batting .216 in 10 postseason games.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wright#cite_note-15)
After the season, Wright participated in the 2006 MLB Japan All-Star Series along with teammates José Reyes, Julio Franco, and John Maine.

## Professional career
### New York Mets (2004–2016, 2018)
As of April 21, 2007, Wright had a hitting streak of 26 regular-season games; the previous team record was 24, held by Mike Piazza and Hubie Brooks. He had a hit in the 12 final regular-season games of the 2006 season, and had a hit in all of the first 14 games of the 2007 season.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wright#cite_note-16) Wright's hit streak of 26 regular-season games ended on April 21, 2007, against the Atlanta Braves at Shea Stadium.
On September 16, 2007, Wright became the 29th player in baseball history to join the 30–30 club, after hitting a 7th inning solo home run against the Philadelphia Phillies at Shea Stadium. He is only the third player to reach this milestone before his 25th birthday, and only the third Met to reach this milestone in club history, the other two being Howard Johnson and Darryl Strawberry.
Wright finished the 2007 season with a .325 batting average, 30 home runs, 107 RBI, and 34 stolen bases. He was awarded the 2007 Gold Glove and the Silver Slugger Award at third base. Wright also was fourth in the NL MVP voting receiving 182 votes.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wright#cite_note-17)
Wright with the Mets in 2008
Wright began the year with two doubles, including a bases-clearing double, in finishing 2–4 with three RBIs in the Mets' Opening Day victory over the Florida Marlins, 7–2. With the RBIs, Wright was already halfway to matching his RBI production from the preceding April. In the final game of the series, Wright went 3–5 with a home run. On April 13, 2008, Wright hit his 100th career home run, a solo shot off of Milwaukee Brewers pitcher Jeff Suppan.

## Professional career

On August 7, Wright hit the first walk-off home run of his career against the San Diego Padres, giving the Mets a 5–3 victory.

In mid-August, when 10 Mets players were on the disabled list, Wright was added to the list after sustaining an injury on August 15. Wright suffered a concussion when he was hit in the head with a 93 mph (150 km/h)fastball by San Francisco Giants pitcher Matt Cain. He was admitted to the Hospital for Special Surgery, where he underwent a precautionary CT scan, which turned out negative.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wright#cite_note-21) The following day, he left the hospital diagnosed with post-concussion symptoms. He was then placed on the disabled list for the first time in his career.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wright#cite_note-22)

Despite the injury to Wright, General Manager Omar Minaya stated that there were no plans to shut him down for the remainder of the season.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wright#cite_note-23) In fact, Wright was activated from the disabled list on September 1 and started at third base against the Colorado Rockies that evening. Every MLB The Show game since MLB 06 has put at least one star on the box. This page lists every cover athlete from MLB 06: The Show through MLB The Show 26, newest first, plus the special edition and regional covers, and what we know so far about MLB The Show 27.
Looking for the in-game cards instead? Every Cover Athlete Series card we track is on our Cover Athletes card series page.

## How MLB The Show Picks Its Cover Athlete
San Diego Studio (SDS) picks one main cover athlete each year, and it's usually a player coming off a big season. Dustin Pedroia (MLB 09), Joe Mauer (MLB 10), Josh Donaldson (MLB The Show 16) and Shohei Ohtani (MLB The Show 22) were all reigning American League MVPs when they got the cover.
It isn't only about stats. When SDS announced Vladimir Guerrero Jr. for MLB The Show 24, it said it looks for "great baseball players who have interesting stories to tell" and people "who genuinely enjoy playing MLB The Show."
The reveal also marks the start of the new game's pre-release cycle. The cover announcement usually comes with the release date, and the special edition reveal follows a few days later.

## MLB The Show cover athlete ranking
### 17) Javier Baez in MLB The Show 20
Baez lands last because the shortened 2020 season went badly both statistically and emotionally. He hit .203 with a .599 OPS across 59 games, a sharp fall from the energetic all around play that made him such a marketable selection. The unusual schedule makes every 2020 comparison imperfect, but the cover season never developed into a convincing success.

## MLB The Show cover athlete ranking
### 16) Jazz Chisholm Jr in MLB The Show 23
San Diego Studio took a reasonable swing on an exciting young player coming off a 2022 All Star selection. Injuries again interrupted Chisholm’s progress, however, and he played only 97 games in 2023. He still approached a 20 home run and 20 stolen base season, so I would call this a miss in timing rather than proof that the player lacked cover appeal.

## MLB The Show cover athlete ranking
### 15) Yasiel Puig in MLB 15 The Show
Puig had already produced an All Star caliber 2014 season worth roughly five wins above replacement, which made the choice less reckless than it can look in hindsight. He appeared in only 79 games in 2015 and posted a .758 OPS. The energy, Los Angeles market, and breakout potential all made sense, but the actual cover year failed to deliver.

## MLB The Show cover athlete ranking
### 14) Joe Mauer in MLB 11 The Show
Mauer received a second consecutive cover, but the second season was the difficult one. Injuries limited him to 82 games, and his production declined across the board. His peak had already justified the larger relationship with the series, yet MLB 11 was the weaker of his two individual cover cases.

## MLB The Show cover athlete ranking
### 13) Adrian Gonzalez in MLB 12 The Show
Gonzalez was pictured in a Boston uniform and ended the season with the Dodgers, which immediately made the artwork feel dated. He still drove in 108 runs and finished with an .806 OPS, but those numbers were modest by his own standard. I also think the selection arrived after his most memorable years in San Diego rather than at the center of his peak.

## MLB The Show cover athlete ranking
### 12) Bryce Harper in MLB The Show 19
Harper’s move from Washington to Philadelphia gave the cover enormous marketing value. His 2019 line included 35 home runs, 114 RBI, an .882 OPS, and about four wins above replacement, but the Phillies finished at .500. It was a strong season for most players and a merely good one for Harper, which keeps the cover in the lower half.

## MLB The Show cover athlete ranking
### 11) Aaron Judge in MLB The Show 18
Judge earned the cover with a historic rookie season that included 52 home runs, Rookie of the Year, and second place in MVP voting. A wrist injury limited him to 112 games in 2018, but he still hit 27 home runs, posted a .919 OPS, and played well in October. The missed time caps the ranking even though the choice itself was excellent.

## MLB The Show cover athlete ranking
### 10) Fernando Tatis Jr in MLB The Show 21
Tatis led the National League with 42 home runs, produced a .975 OPS, and finished third in MVP voting while playing 130 games. San Diego missed the postseason, and later injury and suspension changed the way the period is remembered. Judged only on the 2021 cover year, this was still a well timed selection with elite power at shortstop.

## MLB The Show cover athlete ranking
### 9) Joe Mauer in MLB 10 The Show
Mauer entered the cover year after an extraordinary 2009 MVP season in which he hit .365 with a .444 on base percentage and 1.031 OPS. He remained an elite offensive catcher in 2010, hitting .327 with an .871 OPS and finishing eighth in MVP voting. Combining those two seasons makes the first Mauer cover far stronger than the second.

### 8) Dustin Pedroia in MLB 09 The Show
Pedroia earned the selection with a 2008 MVP season that included 213 hits, 54 doubles, 118 runs, 20 stolen bases, and roughly seven wins above replacement. His 2009 follow up was less spectacular but still valuable, with an .819 OPS and another strong all around season at second base. The cover caught him near the heart of his peak.

### 7) Ryan Howard in MLB 08 The Show
Howard led the majors with 48 home runs and 146 RBI, finished second in National League MVP voting, and helped Philadelphia win the 2008 World Series. His on base percentage and defense prevent the season from rating as highly by modern all around measures, but a championship cover year with that much power deserves a prominent place.

## MLB The Show cover athlete ranking
### 6) Miguel Cabrera in MLB 14 The Show
Cabrera entered 2014 after consecutive MVP awards and the 2012 Triple Crown. The cover season looked quiet only beside that impossible standard: he hit .313 with 25 home runs, 109 RBI, and an .895 OPS while Detroit won its division. I cannot put him lower when the selection represented one of the greatest modern hitting runs.

## MLB The Show cover athlete ranking
### 5) David Ortiz in MLB 06 The Show
Ortiz gave the newly named series an ideal first face. He entered the year as the defining hitter for a Boston team that had just broken its championship drought, then led the American League with 54 home runs, 137 RBI, and 119 walks. He finished third in MVP voting and made the inaugural The Show cover feel immediately important.

## MLB The Show cover athlete ranking
### 4) Josh Donaldson in MLB The Show 16
Donaldson followed his 2015 MVP season with 37 home runs, a .953 OPS, and another campaign near eight wins above replacement. Toronto returned to the American League Championship Series, where he continued to hit. Power, defense, durability, and postseason relevance make this one of the most complete cover windows on the list.

## MLB The Show cover athlete ranking
### 3) David Wright in MLB 07 The Show
Wright delivered the best season of his career at age 24. He hit 30 home runs, stole 34 bases, drove in 107 runs, posted a .963 OPS, and produced roughly eight wins above replacement. He finished fourth in MVP voting, but the combination of offense, defense, speed, age, and the New York stage makes the selection look outstanding.

## MLB The Show cover athlete ranking
### 2) Andrew McCutchen in MLB 13 The Show
McCutchen won the National League MVP, a Gold Glove, and helped Pittsburgh end a 20 season postseason drought. He hit .317 with a .404 on base percentage, 21 home runs, 27 stolen bases, and 7.8 Baseball Reference WAR. The Pirates also advanced beyond the Wild Card Game, giving the cover season individual dominance and franchise meaning.

## MLB The Show cover athlete ranking
### 1) Shohei Ohtani in MLB The Show 22
Ohtani remains my clear choice at number one. He hit 34 home runs with an .875 OPS, then recorded a 2.33 ERA and 219 strikeouts in 166 innings. Baez in 2020, Puig in 2015, Chisholm in 2023, and Mauer in 2011 produced the weakest combinations of health and performance. That does not mean every original decision was poor. Cover artwork is selected before most of the associated season is played, so marketing value, recent production, personality, regional appeal, and release deadlines all matter.
The idea of a cover curse also ignores selection bias. A player is often chosen immediately after a career year, when ordinary regression is already more likely. Injury can then turn an understandable choice into a disappointing result.

## Why Aaron Judge returned for MLB The Show 26
Judge first appeared on MLB The Show 18 after his record setting rookie season. He returned for MLB The Show 26 as a three time American League MVP, this time in a Team USA uniform linked to World Baseball Classic content. Joe Mauer is the other player with two consecutive primary United States covers.
For a wider comparison across sports series, the dominant cover athletes list puts MLB stars beside the leading names from Madden, NBA 2K, NHL, FIFA, and UFC.

## MLB The Show cover athlete ranking
### 3) David Wright in MLB 07 The Show
Wright delivered the best season of his career at age 24. He hit 30 home runs, stole 34 bases, drove in 107 runs, posted a .963 OPS, and produced roughly eight wins above replacement. He finished fourth in MVP voting, but the combination of offense, defense, speed, age, and the New York stage makes the selection look outstanding.

## MLB The Show cover athlete ranking
### 2) Andrew McCutchen in MLB 13 The Show
McCutchen won the National League MVP, a Gold Glove, and helped Pittsburgh end a 20 season postseason drought. He hit .317 with a .404 on base percentage, 21 home runs, 27 stolen bases, and 7.8 Baseball Reference WAR. The Pirates also advanced beyond the Wild Card Game, giving the cover season individual dominance and franchise meaning.
texts.19:
## MLB The Show cover athlete ranking
### 1) Shohei Ohtani in MLB The Show 22
Ohtani remains my clear choice at number one. He hit 34 home runs with an .875 OPS, then recorded a 2.33 ERA and 219 strikeouts in 166 innings. He finished second in American League MVP voting and fourth in Cy Young voting. No other cover athlete in the modern series supplied elite value as both a hitter and pitcher during the same season.
texts.20:
## The biggest cover year misses
Baez in 2020, Puig in 2015, Chisholm in 2023, and Mauer in 2011 produced the weakest combinations of health and performance. That does not mean every original decision was poor. Cover artwork is selected before most of the associated season is played, so marketing value, recent production, personality, regional appeal, and release deadlines all matter.
The idea of a cover curse also ignores selection bias. A player is often chosen immediately after a career year, when ordinary regression is already more likely. Injury can then turn an understandable choice into a disappointing result.

## Why Aaron Judge returned for MLB The Show 26
Judge first appeared on MLB The Show 18 after his record setting rookie season. He returned for MLB The Show 26 as a three time American League MVP, this time in a Team USA uniform linked to World Baseball Classic content. Joe Mauer is the other player with two consecutive primary United States covers.
For a wider comparison across sports series, the dominant cover athletes list puts MLB stars beside the leading names from Madden, NBA 2K, NHL, FIFA, and UFC.

## How MLB The Show Picks Its Cover Athlete
San Diego Studio (SDS) picks one main cover athlete each year, and it's usually a player coming off a big season. Dustin Pedroia (MLB 09), Joe Mauer (MLB 10), Josh Donaldson (MLB The Show 16) and Shohei Ohtani (MLB The Show 22) were all reigning American League MVPs when they got the cover.
It isn't only about stats. When SDS announced Vladimir Guerrero Jr. for MLB The Show 24, it said it looks for "great baseball players who have interesting stories to tell" and people "who genuinely enjoy playing MLB The Show."
The reveal also marks the start of the new game's pre-release cycle. The cover announcement usually comes with the release date, and the special edition reveal follows a few days later.

Griffey's injuries continued in the 2006 off-season. While on holiday in the Bahamas with his family, he broke his wrist.[45] Griffey said his hand felt fine and he expected to be ready to go for 2007 spring training.[61]
2007edit  
Griffey in 2007 with the Reds
At the beginning of the 2007 Major League Baseball season, Ryan Freel took over center field for the Reds, and Griffey Jr. was moved to right field. Reds manager Jerry Narron said, "I've got to do everything I can do to put our best club out there. My feeling is that with Ryan Freel out there, it gives us strong defense up the middle."[62]
On May 10, 2007, Griffey hit his sixth home run of the season and the 569th of his career, tying Rafael Palmeiro for ninth place on the career home runs list.[63] He passed Palmeiro on May 13 against the Los Angeles Dodgers.[64] Griffey tied Harmon Killebrew for eighth on the all-time list hitting his 573rd career home run on May 22.[65] He then surpassed him on May 25 against the Pittsburgh Pirates.[66]

On June 22, 2007, Griffey made his first return to Seattle after his trade to the Reds.[67] Before the game, the Mariners honored him with a 15-minute presentation which included a highlight reel of his playing career with the Mariners, a presentation of a "The House that Griffey Built" memorial by Mariners hall-of-famers and former teammates Jay Buhner and Edgar Martínez, and a four-minute standing ovation from the sold-out crowd.[68][69] Griffey did not expect such a welcome or a turnout by fans when he came back, and a short but emotional speech was given by Griffey afterwards.[68] Many of the fans in attendance made signs professing their gratitude and adoration toward him with quotes such as: "The House that Griffey Built", "Seattle Junior", and "Griffey we miss you."[67] Griffey went 1-for-5 in the game.[68] On June 24, Griffey hit his 583rd and 584th career home runs, tying and passing Mark McGwire for seventh place on the all-time career home run list.[70]
Wow. Never did I imagine that it would be like this coming back. I spent 11 years here, 11 wonderful years here. ... This place will be [my] home. ... I didn't realize how much I missed being in Seattle.
— An excerpt from Griffey's short speech as noted above.[71]
Following the Cincinnati Reds versus Seattle Mariners series from June 22–24, 2007, a fan movement emerged petitioning Mariners' management to bring Griffey back. Over 1,900 signatures were collected on a fan vid-blog/petition.[72]

Griffey received the most votes of any player in the National League for the 2007 All-Star balloting,[73] and in the July 10 game, he went on to drive in two runs for the National League.[74] On July 16, 2007, Griffey hit his 587th home run to pass Frank Robinson for sixth place on the all-time home run list.[75] On July 18, 2007, Griffey hit his 2,500th hit, a first-inning single off Atlanta Braves starting pitcher John Smoltz.[76]
On September 19, 2007, in a game against the Chicago Cubs, Griffey fielded a Derrek Lee single in right field, then suddenly went down in pain.[77] The injury, first thought to be a lower abdominal strain, was later revealed to be a season-ending groin strain. This marked one of many seasons in Cincinnati in which Griffey had to end the year on the disabled list.[78] Griffey ended the 2007 season with 593 career home runs.
On August 22, 2007, Griffey was selected as an all-time Rawlings Gold Glove winner, on a list of nine players considered the greatest defensive players in the last 50 years.[79] He finished the season with 78 runs, 146 hits, 24 doubles, one triple, 30 home runs, 93 RBI, and a .277 batting average in 144 games.[9]
2008edit
On April 4, 2008, Griffey passed Reggie Jackson for 16th on the all-time list after driving in his 1,702nd run.[80] On June 9, Griffey hit his 600th home run on a 3–1 pitch from Mark Hendrickson of the Florida Marlins in the first inning at Land Shark Stadium in Miami. Fans of both teams gave him a standing ovation.[81]

Despite being ranked second in the National League All-Star voting for outfielders for most of the first half of the season, Griffey finished fourth with 2,907,746 ballots, 87,000 votes behind Kosuke Fukudome. He was not selected to the All-Star Game as a reserve. At the All-Star Break, Griffey was batting .239 with 12 home runs and 42 RBI. "I always have a backup plan... If you can't hit a tough lefty, bunt. If you can't hit a tough righty, bunt. If you can't go to the All-Star Game, go to the Bahamas," Griffey said.[82]
On July 30, Griffey hit his 608th career home run in his last game for the Reds.[83]
Griffey was criticized by some for his effort during his stint with the Reds. Gregg Doyel had this to say of the years Griffey was with the Reds in comparison to the 2010 Reds team: "It's a different Reds team than the older, beer-bellied softball teams of recent years. Those Reds were Ken Griffey and Adam Dunn lounging on the clubhouse's leather couches, hitting home runs, misplaying balls in the outfield, and thinking they had it all figured out, when all they knew how to do was lose."[84]
Chicago White Sox (2008)edit  
Ken Griffey Jr. in 2008 with the Chicago White Sox
On July 31, 2008, at the MLB trade deadline, Griffey was traded to the Chicago White Sox for pitcher Nick Masset and infielder Danny Richar, ending his nine-year tenure in Cincinnati.[85][86] In his first game with the White Sox, he went 2-for-3 with 2 RBI, a walk, and a run.[87]
On August 20, 2008, Griffey hit his first home run as a member of the White Sox, off the Mariners' R. A. Dickey, which moved him into a tie with former outfielder Sammy Sosa for fifth place in career home runs.[88] He surpassed Sosa on September 23, with one off Minnesota's Matt Guerrier.[89]

Griffey's signature moment with the White Sox came on September 30, the last game of the 2008 season; an extra 163rd game between the White Sox and Minnesota Twins to break the tie atop the AL Central. In the fifth inning of the scoreless game, the Twins threatened with Michael Cuddyer on third and one out. Twins third baseman Brendan Harris flied out softly to Griffey in center field, who threw a strike to White Sox catcher A. J. Pierzynski, who tagged out Cuddyer at home in a home plate collision to complete the double play and end the threat.[90] The White Sox went on to beat the Twins, 1–0, to advance to the 2008 American League Division Series,[90] where they fell to the Tampa Bay Rays.
On October 30, 2008, the White Sox declined a $16 million option on Griffey, making him a free agent for the first time in his career. Griffey received a buyout for $4 million, split between the Reds and White Sox.[91] Griffey hit .249 with 18 home runs and 71 RBI during 143 games with the Reds and White Sox in 2008.[9][91] When the 2008 season ended he said he wouldn't retire, saying "I've got things to do."[92]
Seattle Mariners (second stint) (2009–2010)edit  
Griffey, batting against the Cubs after returning to the Mariners during Spring training, March 2009.

As a free agent, Griffey was courted by the Mariners and the Atlanta Braves. The national media was dubious about Griffey's ability to contribute meaningfully, with The Washington Post noting "... the Mariners are not about to sign Griffey for baseball reasons; they're bringing him back to Seattle to sell tickets."[93] Griffey ultimately accepted a contract offer from the Mariners on February 18, 2009, after "agonizing" over the decision. Griffey indicated he was motivated by sentimental reasons toward Seattle, where he received an overwhelmingly positive reception when he last played there as a Cincinnati Red in June 2007, but was inclined towards the Braves for its proximity to his home in Orlando, Florida, and his desire to be with his family during the season.[94] Apparently, Griffey was very close to signing with the Braves; however, a premature report emerged from The Atlanta Journal-Constitution that an Atlanta deal was done and a conversation with Willie Mays and his own 13-year-old daughter played a factor in his choice.[95] Griffey once again sported #24 with the Mariners; the team had not issued the number to any player or coach in the nine years between his two stints in Seattle.
Ken Griffey Jr. during his final plate appearance of the 2009 season.
Griffey went 1-for-3 with a home run in his regular-season debut on April against the Minnesota Twins.[96] The home run was Griffey's eighth Opening Day home run;[96] as of 2025, he is tied with Frank Robinson and Adam Dunn for first place in this category. On April 15, 2009, Griffey hit his 400th home run as a Mariner (613th of career), off Los Angeles Angels pitcher Jered Weaver, becoming the first MLB player to hit 400 home runs with one club (Mariners) and 200 home runs with another (Reds).[97] AP stated, "Griffey returned to the Mariners in 2009 and almost single-handedly transformed what had been a fractured, bickering clubhouse with his leadership, energy and constant pranks."[37]

On June 23, 2009, at Safeco Field, Griffey hit the 5,000th home run in franchise history, off San Diego Padres pitcher Chad Gaudin.[98] This was Griffey's 619th career home run. On July 1, Griffey hit career home run 621 at the new Yankee Stadium, off Yankees pitcher Andy Pettitte in the sixth inning.[99] It marked the 44th different ballpark in which he had hit a home run.[99] On August 12, 2009, against his former team, the Chicago White Sox, he hit a run-scoring single in the bottom of the 14th inning to win the game, 1–0, for the Mariners.[100]
Griffey returned to the Mariners for the 2010 campaign with a similar one-year contract to that of 2009,[101] but struggled offensively over the first two months while posting a .184 batting average.[9] On April 27, Griffey passed Andre Dawson for 45th on the career hit list. On May 20, in a game against the Toronto Blue Jays, Griffey hit a run-scoring single off Blue Jays' closer Kevin Gregg to win the game, 4–3, for the Mariners.[102] After starting the ninth inning trailing 3–1, the Mariners rallied in the bottom of the ninth to load the bases on two singles and a walk, then tied the game via a walk and a sacrifice fly.[102] The walk-off single was the final hit and run batted in of Griffey's MLB career, and moved him past Rafael Palmeiro to 14th on the all-time RBI list.
Retirementedit

On January 6, 2016, Griffey was elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame, receiving 99.32 percent of the vote, breaking the record previously held by Tom Seaver's 98.84 percent in 1992.[127] (Mariano Rivera later became the first unanimous inductee in 2019.[128]) A flag bearing Griffey's number 24 was flown from Seattle's Space Needle following the announcement.[129] Griffey is one of four Baseball Hall of Fame inductees who have been chosen first overall in an MLB draft. The other three are Chipper Jones, who was inducted in 2018, Harold Baines, who was inducted by the Veterans Committee in 2019, and Joe Mauer, who was inducted in 2024.[130]
Coinciding with his Hall of Fame election, the Mariners announced on January 8, 2016, that they would retire his jersey number 24. The retirement took effect with the start of the 2016 MLB season, with the formal ceremony taking place prior to the Mariners' August 6 game.[131] The jersey retirement includes the number 24 also being taken out of circulation of all of the Mariners minor league affiliates.[131]
The Mariners also honored Griffey in a unique fashion in the 2016 MLB draft, selecting his son Trey in the 24th round (matching his jersey number), even though Trey, at the time a wide receiver at the University of Arizona, had not played baseball since his preteen years.[132]
On July 29, 2021, Griffey was elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame's Board of Directors.[133]
As of 2021, Griffey is also working as a senior adviser to MLB Commissioner Rob Manfred.[134]
Philanthropyedit

In 2008, Griffey released a series of charity wines to support The Ken Griffey Jr. Family Foundation, a fund that supports several causes, including the Boys & Girls Clubs of America and several children's hospitals across the United States.[135] He is also an honorary co-chairman of the AOPA Foundation's Hat in the Ring Society, a charitable organization that promotes aviation safety and education.[136]

Personal lifeedit
In April 2007, Griffey was diagnosed with pleurisy, an inflammation of the lining of the cavity surrounding the lungs which can cause painful respiration and other symptoms.[137][138]
Griffey and his wife Melissa have three children: Ken Griffey III (Trey), daughter Taryn Kennedy, and son Tevin Kendall. Trey was a wide receiver in the National Football League (NFL) (2017–2019).[139] Taryn attended the University of Arizona and played for the women's basketball team.[140]
The Griffey family resides in Windermere, Florida, where Ken Griffey Sr. also lives.[141][142]
Griffey was named an American Public Diplomacy Envoy by Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice on November 18, 2008.[143]
Griffey has a private pilot certificate and owns a Cirrus SR22.[144]

Since 2015, Griffey has worked as a sports photographer, and has been credentialed to shoot MLB, MLS, NFL, and IndyCar events and the 2025 Masters Tournament.[145][146][147][148]
The video game MLB The Show 17 includes Griffey as the cover athlete for the American version of the game.
The Griffey family joined as a minority owner in the Seattle Sounders FC on November 17, 2020.[149]
On May 26, 2024, Griffey drove the pace car for the Indianapolis 500.[150]
Suicide attemptedit
In January 1988, Griffey attempted suicide by swallowing 277 aspirin pills but wound up in intensive care at Providence Hospital in Mount Airy, Ohio.[151] Griffey Jr. cited arguments with his father, depression, and anger as reasons for his attempted suicide.[152] On his failed attempt, he said, "It seemed like everyone was yelling at me in baseball, then I came home and everyone was yelling at me there. I got depressed. I got angry. I didn't want to live."[152] He stated that he had also previously contemplated taking his own life, but he had not acted on it until this incident.[152] After Griffey swallowed the aspirin, his girlfriend's mother drove him to the hospital.[152] While in intensive care, he ripped the IV from his arm in order to stop an argument between him and his father.[152] Both Griffey and his father stated that the incident changed their relationship, and since then, there has been better understanding for both of them.[152]
